Headline: AAII Bears Retreat Even as Stocks Slide

Bearishness in the AAII sentiment survey eased to 42.2% this week from 51.4% last week, when it topped 50% for the first time in eight weeks. Bullishness edged up to 33.3% from 30.8%, and neutral sentiment jumped to 24.4% from 17.8%.

That narrowed the bull-bear spread to −8.9 from −20.6 and lifted the bull/bear ratio to 0.79 from 0.60, though it remains below its 1.18 long-run average, with bears still well above their 31.5% historical average and bulls below their 37.5%.

What stands out is the timing. Retail investors got less bearish over a stretch in which the S&P 500 fell 3.5% (Thursday to Wednesday, the survey period) and closed below its November 5th low.

Last week’s spread below −20 was the kind of reading DB notes has typically been followed by gains (S&P higher a month later 68% of the time, median +2.8%, since 2010), so some of that contrarian cushion has now been used up.

The caveat: Looking back to 1990, in the 17 years when VIX started mid-November at 18 or higher, as it does now, it was lower by year-end in 14, by -3.25 pts on average. In those same years SPX's year-end gain was smaller (mean +1.34%, up in 59% of years). 

As outlined above, the period usually sees a dip first – the median drawdown within the window is -3.0%. Additionally, most of the gains come late; from Dec 15th to year-end the mean is +1.22%, and SPX rose in 27 of 36 years

Markets have now given me PTSD on every green rally.

That being said, $SOI accelerating from $25m quarterly photonics-SOI revenue… with no forward visibility earlier this year.

Into securing $1.2B in agreements this quarter, backed by cash, is extremely transformative and make me happy to see.

In terms transcript details:

- “AI data center have built large compute power, but some of it remains idle as copper links limit data availability for processing. 

Optics removes that bottleneck”

Reiterating what I said about aggregate capex not applying 1:1 with optical sector, given optical shifts improves GPU utilization

- timelines: “Near-package optics brings first volume by the end of the fiscal year, and high volume next year. 

Co-Packaged Optics for scale out is starting to ramp. TPO for scale up will be the next stage”

- “Growth comes in waves, scale out and scale up as a new driver. As those links goes optical, they create new volume on top of today's. 

In fiscal year 2027, our revenue comes mostly from pluggable transceiver, and we see initial volume from NPO.”

- “Growth returned sooner than we had anticipated and with more vigor. Revenue grew 39%, with Photonics-SOI leading the way.

Margin expansion has come forward too”

- “So, for the capacity reservation agreement we signed, they cover calendar year 2027, calendar year 2028, and beyond”

In terms of where they see acceleration:

- “Now we see and we believe the new requests that we are getting lately are more for the Co-Packaged Optics and NPO. And especially for the scale-up going forward.”

I think that this quarter earnings marks the inflection of optical acceleration for Soitec + silicon photonics.

And what it means for a chokepoint to transform into company economics.

Biggest issue with the PEARL pitch is that BTC failing (I would assume if something could flip Bitcoin that the market cap of BTC had dropped drastically) would be such devastating capital destruction that it undermines the idea that a digital SOV can work. 

The idea would be cemented that there will always be another digital SOV to vamp whatever is popular and current. These assets would therefore remain very niche and unlikely to be popular with global investors or big capital again. 

So, I think this pitch is wrong, even there are aspects of the design that are superior and interesting, but I get that saying “PEARL can flip BTC” is the way you get attention, and draw people in. 

We have had very few liquid SOVs in the modern world, and for good reason, it’s extremely difficult for something to manage to durably compete over a long time horizon with the existing old few SOVs that we have. 

BTC still has a very long way to go in its attempt to offer a credible alternative to a 5000 year old coveted shiny rock.

BTC succeeding and continuing to rise in value is good for all alt digital SOVs.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the daily metals pulse.

1. @OpenBot_

I replaced GrokBot with OpenBot 2 weeks ago - best decision I've made in months. 

After the whole usage issue a few weeks ago, I knew I couldn't rely on Grok anymore. 

I didn't want to end up in a situation where I have shit to do, and Grok rugpulls me with the usage or replaces it with an idiotic model to save on costs. 

I tried out a few and Openbot's my fav.  It runs on my Claude subscription, so I'm always on a frontier model instead of whatever GrokBot picks under the hood. 

And my usage issues are gone.

OpenBot runs locally on my Mac mini. 

Even though people view OpenBot as a GrokBot replacement - it's starting to add new features which makes it even better imo. 

threaded conversation, agent docks, library, etc. 

2. Claude: $200/mo Ultra plan

My main model. I use Opus 5.5 day to day and switch to Fable 5.2 for the hardest problems.

No explanation needed, Claude's simply the best. 

3. ChatGPT: $20/mo

I mainly use it for image generation and whenever I want a second opinion. 

4. GrokBot: $30/mo

The one thing I can't replace is Grok's native X integration for research.

So I run GrokBot as a bot inside OpenBot:

• My OpenBot agent sends my message to GrokBot over a webhook.
• Grok does the work and drops its answer into a shared folder on my Mac mini.
• My agent reads it back to me.

So, it feels like chatting with any other bot.

5. OpenRouter: pay as you go

One account and one API key give me pay-as-you-go access to the models I don't subscribe to, like Gemini, Qwen, Kimi and Grok. 

They mostly power my Mixture of Agents skill, and my agent switches each one to its newest version every week.

Say you're making a huge decision. Ask Claude and you get one answer. But what if you could get several perspectives from different AI models and end up with the best version?

a. Fast mode: Claude writes one version and ChatGPT writes another, without seeing each other's. Gemini grades both and picks the winner. Then my agent writes the final version from the winner, adding the best points from the runner-up.

b. Full mode: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, Kimi and Grok each write their own answer, and so does my agent. They grade each other's work blind, never their own. 

A model that didn't write the top answer turns it into the final version. Then Grok, whose job is to disagree, tears it apart before I see it.

Fast takes a few minutes and costs cents. Full takes about half an hour and a few dollars, so I save it for the big calls.

Everything's moving so fast so it'll probably end up looking different next year.

Anyways I spent a lot of time testing diff things out and reached a setup I'm very happy with.

India is the only place I've felt genuine 'culture shock'. I spent a good few months there when I was younger, with little money, and this was my experience

The first word I think of, when I think of India is overwhelming. In almost every sense:

- The diversity and flavour of the food
- The celebration and visibility of religion and spirituality
- The importance of, and passion for, cricket
- The density of people, noise and traffic
- The scale and proximity of inequality
- The intensity of social interaction, from negotiating everything to the directness of personal questions
- The warm and welcoming nature of the people and their desire to share their culture, both nationally and locally
- The chaotic nature of everyday life, where everything feels co-ordinated in its own disorganisation

Overall, I think India is best understood through its contradictions, both in individual places and across states. One of the biggest of these is how incredibly warm people are individually, and yet how impersonal things can feel in the aggregate, where bureaucratic systems are a nightmare and corruption is commonplace

I remember waiting for a bus and asking a guy at the bus stop when it would arrive. 'Soon, don't worry' A couple of hours passed, so I asked again. 'Soon, my friend' Eventually it got dark, and I asked him one final time. 'Ah, it comes tomorrow. Let's go eat something, macha?'

It's that sort of thing that takes a while to adjust to. Indians seem to have an insanely high tolerance for chaos, and you've got to learn to rely on adjust karna. The idea that you will simply accommodate delays and changes as they happen

It's the type of place you're so happy you've been to, but have a sense of relief when you leave

I imagine that as a tourist with money, you'll experience many of the same things but remain more insulated from them, becoming more of an observer. If you go, go see the beauty of the country but also try to talk to people and experience some of everyday life. The people and communities is what makes India so distinctive

One day I'll probably go back and see it more from this POV. For now it remains a country I have a lot of love for, even if that love is complicated

India is the only place I've felt genuine 'culture shock'. I spent a good few months there when I was younger, with little money, and this was my experience

The first word I think of, when I think of India is overwhelming. In almost every sense:

- The diversity and flavour of the food
- The celebration and visibility of religion and spirituality
- The importance of, and passion for, cricket
- The density of people, noise and traffic
- The scale and proximity of inequality
- The intensity of social interaction, from negotiating everything to the directness of personal questions
- The warm and welcoming nature of the people and their desire to share their culture, both nationally and locally
- The chaotic nature of everyday life, where everything feels co-ordinated in its own disorganisation

Overall, I think India is best understood through its contradictions, both in individual places and across states. One of the biggest of these is how incredibly warm people are individually, and yet how impersonal things can feel in the aggregate, where bureaucratic systems are a nightmare and corruption is commonplace

I remember waiting for a bus and asking a guy at the bus stop when it would arrive. 'Soon, don't worry' A couple of hours passed, so I asked again. 'Soon, my friend' Eventually it got dark, and I asked him one final time. 'Ah, it comes tomorrow. Let's go eat something, macha?'

It's that sort of thing that takes a while to adjust to. Indians seem to have an insanely high tolerance for chaos, and you've got to learn to rely on adjust karna. The idea that you will simply accommodate delays and changes as they happen

It's the type of place you're so happy you've been to, but have a sense of relief when you leave

I imagine that as a tourist with money, you'll experience many of the same things but remain more insulated from them, becoming more of an observer. If you go, go see the beauty of the country but also try to talk to people and experience some of everyday life. The people and communities is what makes India so distinctive

One day I'll probably go back and see it more from this POV. For now it remains a country I have a lot of love for, even if that love is complicated

Worth noting - this is my experience as a man. And I'm sure many women have an incredible, but very different experience of India, particularly when it comes to safety and the freedom to move around independently. That's not something I can speak to myself, but worth bearing in mind if you do visit

I genuinely agree with this take, and don't know why there's so much conflict about it. As much as BTC still drives altcoin movements today, it is quite clear that the trend is weakening and will continue to weaken. And that is a good thing. Hyperliquid & Venice both up >100% YTD within a muted BTC environment.

What we all want is a bifurcation of the market where digital-equity-esque assets are unencumbered by digital SoV price movements. The truth is it, that as the industry continues to print out once-a-year generational companies that are high-growth, make recurring money, and decide to launch a token, that these BUSINESSES should not have their fundamental performance tied to the price of a digital rock which trades based solely on flows and not on fundamentals

A better example would be if the price-action of equities was wholly dependent on how Gold traded. These two assets should move *independently* of each other. Of course, they are usually linked by macro-economic conditions - e.g Gold going up = economic uncertainty so flight to store of value = usually means equities are not doing too hot

But it's more pointing to a simpler fact that Gold should not determine (emphasis on determine here) how equities trade, i.e it's not a cause and effect relationship

However, for most digital assets, Bitcoin is a direct cause and effect relationship across the broader backdrop of the market. And that has made sense considering that for the past 5+ years, Bitcoin was seen as a risk-asset alongside the broader crypo-economic class as well. Bitcoin was touted as a store of value, but in reality, was really just an altcoin, and then altcoins were extremely high beta bitcoins.

However, the relationship now should and has begun to change, because Bitcoin is no longer being treated in the same vein as altcoins. Yes, it is still very much a risk assets in some regimes. But it in many ways has become institutionalized, and that usually leads to lower volatility (-50% drawdown from the 2025 top rather than a -80% drawdown from the 2021 top);  and conversely, you can also imagine that there will be lesser upside volatility as well.

Trad institutions I talk to see Bitcoin as this unironic gold-alternative-with-high-beta-and-asymmetric-upside that they only buy if they think Gold is going to go up, or if it gets cheap enough, or if they think the crypto market has some reason to do well.

Whereas, digital-assets like Hyperliquid, have way more going for it than that. And so, it is natural to want and even to bet on this de-correlating relationship. After all, if Hyperliquid manages to onbaord traditional equities, and their usage doubles, why should the price action of Bitcoin matter? All that matters for Hyperliquid is how the underlying business performs - Bitcoin going up is just an added tailwind, not the necessary ingredient.

And then you extend this logic to the handful of crypto-token-businesses that exist today, and you basically arrive at Jeff's take! I would like to bet on more good crypto-businesses with a token because their business is good, not because I believe Bitcoin can go up.

Okay, so you are talking about the VPL EyePhone, which was designed over 40 years ago and itself an improved copy of a NASA system.  It was about as different from the Rift as a headset could possibly be - multiple displays, several lenses per eye to correct for optical distortion, heavy as a result.  The Rift was a big deal because I figured out how to use one display total feeding one lens for each eye, combined with software-based distortion correction that cost nothing to manufacture.  That is why the EyePhone HRX cost $49, 000 in the 80s (~$150k today) and the Rift was $299. 

The Oculus Rift did not cause nausea, either.  It was a notable breakthrough in that regard.  It was of course still very possible to develop games and experiences that make the player sick, but that is a content decision, not a headset problem.

If you don't like me, you can just say so!  You don't have to make things up!
